mcqs.question: What does a low arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) suggest about a workload?
options: It's more likely to be memory-bound, since it does relatively little math per byte fetched
It's almost certainly compute-bound
It has no bearing on whether the workload is compute- or memory-bound
It means the workload has a bug
mcqs.explanation: Low arithmetic intensity means lots of data movement relative to computation, which pushes the workload's roofline point toward the memory-bandwidth-limited region. It's a direct, meaningful signal about the likely bottleneck, not noise or a sign of a defect.

mcqs.question: On a roofline plot, a workload's point sits directly under the diagonal (memory-bandwidth) line, well below the flat compute-ceiling line. What does this indicate?
options: The workload is compute-bound and needs more ALU throughput
The workload is memory-bound — it's constrained by data movement, not by compute capacity
The workload has zero arithmetic intensity
The hardware has no memory bandwidth limit at all
mcqs.explanation: Sitting under the memory-bandwidth slope (rather than up near the compute ceiling) is exactly the signature of a memory-bound workload — bandwidth is the binding constraint. It isn't necessarily zero intensity (that would place it at the origin), and the plot's slope existing at all confirms the hardware does have a finite bandwidth limit.

mcqs.question: A dot product of two N-element float32 vectors performs 2N FLOPs and moves 8N bytes. What is its arithmetic intensity, and what does that value typically imply?
options: 4 FLOPs/byte — typically compute-bound
2 FLOPs/byte — typically balanced
0.25 FLOPs/byte — typically memory-bound
8 FLOPs/byte — always compute-bound regardless of hardware
mcqs.explanation: 2N / 8N = 0.25 FLOPs/byte, a low value indicating very little computation relative to data moved — the textbook signature of a memory-bound kernel. It is not compute-bound, balanced, or a value that guarantees any bound "always" regardless of the actual hardware's ceilings, though 0.25 is low enough to be memory-bound on virtually every real system.

mcqs.question: A workload is diagnosed as memory-bound on the roofline plot. Why does adding wider vector (SIMD) units fail to speed it up?
options: SIMD units only work on compute-bound workloads by design
Memory-bound workloads cannot be run on any hardware with vector units
SIMD units actually slow down memory-bound workloads
Wider vector units raise the compute ceiling, but the workload is already limited by memory bandwidth, which those units don't change
mcqs.explanation: The roofline point for a memory-bound workload sits under the bandwidth slope, not near the compute ceiling — so raising the compute ceiling (more/wider ALUs) doesn't move the achievable performance at all, since bandwidth was the binding constraint the whole time. SIMD isn't restricted to compute-bound code by design, doesn't inherently slow anything down, and memory-bound code runs fine on vector-capable hardware — it just doesn't benefit from the vector width.

mcqs.question: A GPU has 20 TFLOP/s peak compute and 800 GB/s peak bandwidth, giving a ridge point of 25 FLOPs/byte. A workload with arithmetic intensity 0.25 FLOPs/byte runs on it. What does this tell you?
options: The workload is deeply memory-bound (100x below the ridge point), so adding more compute throughput would not help at all
The workload is compute-bound, so vectorizing the math further would help most
The ridge point is irrelevant once actual performance is measured
The workload's arithmetic intensity will automatically increase to match the ridge point
mcqs.explanation: Being far below the ridge point (0.25 vs 25 FLOPs/byte) means the workload hits the memory-bandwidth ceiling long before it could ever tax peak compute -- adding more compute units does nothing for a memory-bound workload. The fix is reducing bytes moved or improving data reuse, not vectorizing math.

mcqs.question: A naive (untiled) matrix multiply and a cache-blocked (tiled) matrix multiply compute the exact same total FLOPs. Why can one be memory-bound and the other compute-bound?
options: Arithmetic intensity is a fixed property of the algorithm's math, unaffected by implementation
Tiling changes the total number of FLOPs the algorithm performs
Untiled matmul always runs on different, slower hardware than tiled matmul
Arithmetic intensity depends on bytes moved from memory, not just FLOPs computed; tiling increases data reuse in cache, reducing bytes moved and raising intensity
mcqs.explanation: Arithmetic intensity is FLOPs divided by bytes moved, and tiling changes only the bytes-moved term by improving cache reuse -- the FLOP count is identical either way. This is why intensity depends on how code is written, not just what math it computes, and why cache blocking can move the exact same computation from memory-bound to compute-bound.
